text: Instead of trapping something in place and cooling it down, photonic quantum computing sends information racing through optical circuits at the speed of light — and that single design choice changes almost everything about what's hard and what's easy.

A photonic qubit stores its zero and one states in some measurable property of a single photon. Common encodings include polarization, path — which of two waveguides the photon travels down — and time-bin, whether it arrives in an early or late time slot. A separate family, continuous-variable encoding, carries information in the quadratures of squeezed light instead of a discrete two-level system. Whichever encoding is used, photons don't interact with their thermal environment the way charge or spin qubits do, so photonic circuits can run at or near room temperature — no cryostat, no multi-day cooldown.

Here's what that fabrication actually looks like — a silicon wafer holding photonic quantum computing chips, made with semiconductor-style manufacturing techniques borrowed directly from the conventional chip industry. That shared manufacturing base is part of why photonic approaches have a plausible path to large-scale production.

Single-qubit operations are carried out with linear optical elements — beamsplitters that mix two paths, and phase shifters that delay one path relative to another — mature, well-understood components. The harder problem is two-qubit gates, because photons don't naturally interact with each other the way charged particles do. Some architectures use genuine optical nonlinearities; others perform two-photon gates probabilistically, using an extra detection event called heralding to confirm a gate succeeded, discarding and retrying the ones that didn't. And here's the central engineering problem: a photon that's absorbed, scattered, or misdirected is simply gone. There's no storing a lost photon and observing where it went — which is why photon loss, not decoherence in the usual sense, is the dominant error source in photonic systems.

Next lesson: the two companies that dominate the public conversation about photonic quantum computing — PsiQuantum's long manufacturing-scale bet, and Xanadu's cloud-accessible hardware available today.
